title: The War Widens
subtitle: Luga, Staraya Russa and the defence of Odessa
author: R.G. Cruise
phase: II — The Drive into the Soviet Interior
summary: Fighting at Luga, Soviet attacks near Staraya Russa and the defence of Odessa created competing demands for troops and supplies. Success in one sector could tie down forces needed elsewhere.
body:
On 12 August 1941, the Soviet 11th Army was supposed to begin recovering the approaches to Staraya Russa, south of Lake Ilmen. Its plan specified successive river lines, the formations responsible for the main and supporting attacks, and the bridgeheads that following troops must secure. The army was also to prevent German formations from moving against its neighbours. Even before the first objective was reached, therefore, success could take two forms: territory recovered and enemy troops compelled to remain where they were. Holding German formations in this sector could affect operations elsewhere, because the same mobile units were being called upon to meet demands hundreds of kilometres apart. [1] Odessa presented a related strategic problem under different geographical conditions. The Southern Front’s retreat exposed the port to Romania’s 4th Army, while Moscow required its continued defence with the Black Sea Fleet. Loss of land connections could therefore leave a viable route for supply and reinforcement by sea. Read alongside the operations south of Lake Ilmen, the coastal battle reveals how the widening campaign created commitments that could not be resolved by continued forward movement alone. The chapter examines the forces, transport and local knowledge needed to sustain those commitments, together with the civilians whose work and decisions formed part of each defended region. [2]

The northern offensive encounters a system of defences

Army Group North’s advance toward Leningrad involved three connected but distinct tasks. Georg von Küchler’s 18th Army had to clear the Baltic coastal region and Estonia. Erich Hoepner’s 4th Panzer Group supplied the principal mobile striking force toward Leningrad. Ernst Busch’s 16th Army protected the eastern side of the advance, including the region around Lake Ilmen. The army group’s commander, Wilhelm Ritter von Leeb, could concentrate on the city only if these operations supported one another. A successful thrust northward that left Soviet forces on its southeastern flank would lengthen vulnerable communications while reducing the troops available to protect them. [3] The Luga defensive region connected prepared positions to the roads and crossings south and southwest of Leningrad. Forests and difficult ground channelled vehicles and supporting artillery, making a limited number of approaches especially important. A bridgehead required more than troops on the opposite bank: engineers, ammunition and infantry had to reach it through usable routes. During the July delay, Soviet defenders strengthened the region while German infantry approached the armour. The next advance thus confronted a more organised defence whose strength came from the relationship between positions, terrain and reinforcement. Breaking one part of it would not automatically open every route towards the city. [4] The renewed offensive broadened during the second week of August. Blau’s operational account dates the general three-pronged effort to 10 August, distinguishing the advance north from the Ilmen region, the attack from the Luga area, and the western approach. These were converging operations, not three columns moving at a common speed. The formations encountered different defensive positions and could not exchange support freely across the intervening terrain. In particular, an advance toward Novgorod, at the northern end of Lake Ilmen, had implications for the eastern communications of the Luga defenders as well as for the route farther north. [4] The Soviet northern defence also faced pressure from Finland. The Finnish offensive on the Karelian Isthmus had begun on 31 July, while operations east of Lake Ladoga created another demand on Soviet forces. German expectations that the Finns would advance promptly toward the Svir underestimated the problems of their exposed flank and Soviet forces in the Lake Onega region. Finland’s campaign was related to German strategy, but it did not operate as a mechanically synchronised northern pincer. On both sides, the availability of units in one sector depended on decisions and resistance elsewhere. [4]

Staraya Russa and the vulnerable flank

South of Lake Ilmen, the fighting around Staraya Russa exposed the practical meaning of flank protection. The town connected roads and railways through a region divided by the Lovat, Polist, Redya and smaller rivers. Soviet troops east and south of the town could threaten German communications supporting the advance farther north. For the German 16th Army, control of the town therefore required more than possession of its buildings. Forces had to hold the approaches, keep crossings usable, and prevent a Soviet thrust from turning the rear of the units already committed around it. [1] The 11th Army’s journal gives unusually direct evidence of how this struggle was experienced at headquarters. On 3 August it recorded German pressure along the Shimsk road and a penetration near the railway, followed by Soviet efforts to restore the position. Air attacks damaged the line near Pola station and cut wires from Staraya Russa. The army command post was bombed three times. Requests for fighter cover had not been satisfied. A headquarters could issue coherent instructions while losing the communications needed to discover whether those instructions had reached the troops or remained possible. [1] The journal’s account for 4 August attributed German success to artillery, mortars and effective cooperation between aircraft and ground troops, while acknowledging the failure of some Soviet units to hold. This was an interested explanation by a command assessing its reverses, but its detail identifies the mechanisms at work. Fire disrupted formations, damaged communications and complicated movement behind the line. The same entry described Staraya Russa burning under long-range artillery bombardment. The town’s role as a junction connected the military effort to civilian exposure: routes needed for reinforcement and supply also concentrated danger around the places through which inhabitants moved. [1] By 10 August the situation had deteriorated further. The German thrust along the Staraya Russa–Ramushevo road had disorganised the 254th Rifle Division, whose commander was reported to have lost control by the evening. Its withdrawal toward the Lovat created an urgent need to restore order before renewed offensive action. The sequence is revealing: the counterattack of 12 August was not being prepared by an army resting intact behind a secure line. Some of the formations assigned to attack were simultaneously recovering from defeat, rebuilding communications and trying to retain the crossings through which their next movement would pass. [1]

Seven tanks in an army’s daily record

The 11th Army journal recorded seven KV tanks arriving for the 163rd Division on 3 August. In its entry for the next day, it referred to eight KVs available to the army command and their employment with the 22nd Rifle Corps. These were small groups in an army whose responsibilities extended across several river lines. The two figures describe different dated entries and should not be flattened into a single, supposedly exact tank strength. Their significance is the attention headquarters gave to a handful of heavy vehicles while requesting air cover and shifting infantry between threatened sectors. The record does not tell us what each crew thought or how many vehicles remained serviceable after every engagement. It does show that the practical scale of reinforcement could be very different from the massed armoured formations implied by a campaign map. [1]

The counterstroke of 12 August

The plan signed by Vasily Morozov, the 11th Army commander, and his staff prescribed a main attack on the army’s left toward Mavrino and Vyachkovo. The 254th Rifle Division and the 163rd and 202nd motorised formations were assigned to this effort, with the 21st Motorised Rifle Regiment following. A supporting attack by the 22nd Rifle Corps would move from the Parfino direction toward Staraya Russa. The 180th and 183rd Rifle Divisions were to lead there, while the 182nd followed along the main road. This distribution sought to apply pressure across the German position rather than feed every available formation into one narrow approach. [1] The timetable connected successive river problems to the recovery of Staraya Russa. It called for the Redya line on 12 August, further positions including the Porusya on the thirteenth, the town’s eastern part and the Polist on the fourteenth, and the town and Dolzhitsy front by the end of the fifteenth. These remained ordered stages. Each assumed that the preceding crossing could continue serving troops and supplies as the leading formations moved on. The schedule therefore exposes the depth of coordination required from an army whose starting positions were unsettled and whose communications had already suffered serious damage. [1] The second-echelon formations had a dual responsibility. They were to hold bridgeheads and protect crossings successively on the Lovat, Redya, Polist and Porusya, while also reinforcing the attack when circumstances permitted. That assignment connected the forward battle with supply. An attacking regiment could cross a river before its artillery, ammunition transport or casualty evacuation arrangements were secure. Leaving troops at the crossings reduced the immediate striking force but protected the means of sustaining it. The order recognised this tension explicitly. It also left final divisional tasks dependent on the fighting of 11 August, an acknowledgment that the starting position itself was still unsettled. [1] The larger counterstroke involved the 34th Army moving into the gap south of Staraya Russa while the 11th fixed German troops around the town. Robert Forczyk’s account identifies a gap of approximately forty-eight kilometres between the German X and II Corps and describes the resulting danger to the 30th and 290th Infantry Divisions. German commanders responded by sending Erich von Manstein’s LVI Motorised Corps, including the SS Totenkopf formation, against the penetration. The German counterattack began on 19 August. Its success subsequently forced Soviet troops back toward the Lovat. These later events establish both the seriousness of the Soviet threat and its limits; they were not completed outcomes on the chapter’s anchor date. [5] The Soviet operation affected the sequence of German action even though its gains were not retained. Mobile formations were redirected to restore communications and secure the flank of the northern advance, and Hitler ordered an armoured corps transferred from Army Group Centre in response to the danger. Resources considered for a renewed central effort were consequently drawn into another sector’s emergency. The operational effect lay in compelling this redistribution and the fighting required to make the northern position usable again. It must be weighed alongside the Soviet losses incurred when the German response developed, rather than treated as an uncomplicated success measured solely by the diversion achieved. [4]

From the Dniester toward Odessa

In the south, the destruction of the Soviet grouping around Uman had altered the balance without resolving the campaign. As the previous chapter explains, the final resistance there continued beyond the date attached to many accounts of the German victory. Farther south, the Southern Front had to withdraw while preserving enough cohesion to defend new positions. The coastal army protecting Odessa faced a separate requirement: remain near the port while neighbouring forces moved away. Its commander, Georgy Sofronov, could not simply match the retreat of the rest of the front without abandoning the task Moscow had assigned. [3] [2] Romania’s 4th Army under Nicolae Ciupercă approached from the Dniester region. Its movement toward Odessa carried the war beyond the recovery of territories lost by Romania to the Soviet Union in 1940. Romanian forces remained participants in the Axis campaign, with their own command structure and the political ambitions of Ion Antonescu shaping their employment. The operational directive issued on 8 August ordered the 4th Army to defeat Soviet forces between the Dniester and the Tiligul estuary and occupy Odessa. The distance to the objective could be covered more quickly than the defending army could be destroyed. [6] The cost of the approach was already visible at regimental level. Colonel Raoul Halunga’s 10th Vânători Regiment, in the 15th Infantry Division, had crossed the Dniester and fought around Sibka in early August. A museum study based partly on his surviving service documents records repeated Soviet counterattacks and substantial losses in this period. His regiment’s experience demonstrates why the phrase “advance on Odessa” should not imply an uninterrupted march. The fighting before the city’s principal defensive positions consumed the same infantry and leadership that would be needed for the assault. [6] The relationship between retreat and defence can be followed in the Southern Front’s own orders. Directive 0049/op prescribed a staged withdrawal, an intermediate line to be reached by 10 August and a more distant line by the twelfth. It instructed the Coastal Army to begin its withdrawal on the night of 7–8 August toward Berezovka, Katarzhino, Razdelnaya and the Kuchurgan estuary, covered by strong rearguards. The same document required the removal of weapons and equipment from the Rybnitsa and Tiraspol fortified regions. Moving soldiers eastward was only part of the task; valuable matériel also had to be recovered before the roads and crossings disappeared. [7] The withdrawal directive required a sequence that retreat under pressure made difficult to control. Rearguards had to delay pursuit while retaining ammunition and a route for their own departure. Equipment from fixed positions had to be dismantled or loaded before transport connections disappeared. Another line then needed troops ready to receive the retreating formations. Requests for acknowledgements and reports on the start of movement were intended to establish whether that sequence was underway. Odessa’s defence developed within these overlapping tasks, as the coastal army adjusted to the movement of neighbouring forces while preserving the means to hold the port. [7]

A port could remain connected after its land routes closed

Stavka’s directive of 5 August had rejected Budenny’s proposed withdrawal line on the Ingul and specified a more forward position. It also distinguished the immediate withdrawal line from a deeper defensive line, some one hundred to one hundred and fifty kilometres farther back. This was an attempt to preserve space and time rather than surrender both in a single movement. Within that instruction, Odessa received an exceptional obligation: it was to be defended to the limit, with the Black Sea Fleet involved. The port would remain a defended projection west of the larger Soviet withdrawal. [2] Rear Admiral Gavriil Zhukov commanded the Odessa naval base, while Vice Admiral Filipp Oktyabrsky commanded the Black Sea Fleet. Sofronov’s army and the naval establishment consequently had related responsibilities under different immediate chains of command. The distinction mattered because the defence required coastal artillery, ships, infantry, transport and port facilities to work together. On 19 August, a week after this chapter’s anchor date, the Odessa Defence Region would place the combined local defence under Zhukov. That later reorganisation should not be read backward as an arrangement already fully in place on 12 August. [8] By mid-August Romanian troops were completing Odessa’s isolation by land. The ELAR historical account dates the final coastal closure to 13 August. The important distinction for 12 August is that isolation was developing, not that an entirely closed and stable siege ring had existed throughout the preceding week. Nor did a land ring end the port’s connections with the Soviet war effort. Sea transport offered a route for supplies, reinforcements and evacuation, while naval artillery could support the ground defence. The attacking army therefore faced a defended coastal position whose endurance depended partly on a service it could not defeat through infantry advance alone. [9] [4] Comparison with Uman clarifies the importance of the remaining supply route. The armies around Podvysokoye had reported exhausted resources and difficulty receiving help by air. Odessa retained a maritime connection that the defending command was required to employ. Its value depended on ships reaching the port, loads being discharged and supplies moving onwards to the fighting troops. Those stages remained exposed to attack, but they gave the garrison possibilities unavailable to a pocket cut off from ordinary transport. The military meaning of encirclement therefore depended on the functioning connections left open, rather than solely on the territory held around a position. [10] [2]

Civilian work and civilian exposure

The northern journal’s account of Staraya Russa burning reminds us that a road junction was also a place where people lived. Artillery registered on entrances and exits because those routes served troop movement. The resulting danger extended to residents trying to obtain food, reach relatives or leave the town. A railway damaged near the front could interrupt military supply and civilian flight simultaneously. These effects followed from the documented pattern of bombardment; they should not be converted into a precise evacuation total where the record supplies none. The same military geography that explains the battle also explains why escape could become difficult before complete encirclement. [1] Odessa’s civilians also constructed defences and kept workshops operating. That labour connected the garrison’s endurance to households facing bombing and decisions about evacuation. The existence of a sea route must be distinguished from a particular family’s access to it: military transport capacity alone does not establish how many civilians could leave, or when they could do so. [9]

Production and family life

A room beside his father’s workshop

Interviewed by Centropa in February 2003, Mikhail Gauzner recalled his father remaining with workers who produced mine housings after the main plant had been evacuated from Odessa. As bombing intensified, Mikhail and his mother moved into a small room beside his father’s office. The workplace became a place where the family could remain together while defensive production continued. These are a child’s experiences recalled decades later, without a secure day-by-day chronology. The narrow episode links industrial work to domestic decisions and danger; it does not establish what every Odessa household could do or place the move specifically on 12 August.

[11]
Gauzner’s recollection restores a Jewish household to the history of the city’s defence before occupation and persecution became dominant in accounts of its fate. His father’s work, his mother’s decision and the family’s need for proximity connect production to personal circumstances. They also resist treating civilian participation as evidence of a uniform political outlook. Commitment, obligation, professional responsibility and family needs could intersect differently for different people. The value of the testimony lies in the specific relationship it describes, leaving other residents’ motives and opportunities to be established through their own evidence.

Strategy and the international supply question

On 12 August Hitler issued a supplement to Directive 34. Army Group South was to prevent a continuous Soviet defensive line on the Dnieper, seize Crimea and pursue the industrial regions around the Donets and Kharkov. Army Group Centre was to eliminate dangerous flank positions and rehabilitate its armoured forces before an offensive toward Moscow. The northern operation received a decisive place in this sequence: the Leningrad battle was to be brought to a successful conclusion, and the VIII Air Corps returned to the central sector, before the Moscow offensive began. The directive offered conditional opportunities whose requirements competed with one another. [4] The distribution of aviation made the competition for support especially visible. Aircraft could move between sectors more rapidly than infantry armies, but their use still required bases, fuel, maintenance and target information. Concentration on one operation reduced what could immediately be provided elsewhere. The 11th Army’s unanswered requests for fighter cover reveal the effect of those allocation decisions at a lower level: a command could identify a pressing requirement without possessing the authority or resources to satisfy it. Strategic prioritisation acquired practical meaning through such uneven provision, shaping the risks formations had to accept during both attack and defence. [4] [1] Western diplomacy was beginning to turn the Soviet supply problem into an international undertaking, although promises still preceded deliveries. Roosevelt and Churchill met at the Atlantic Conference on 9–12 August. Their joint message proposing further consultation on Soviet needs reached Stalin through the American and British ambassadors on 15 August. The timing matters: these diplomatic steps could influence expectations and procurement, but they could not have equipped the counterattacking armies at Staraya Russa three days earlier. Britain was already a belligerent against Germany; the United States was assisting resistance to the Axis while remaining outside formal war with Germany. [12] Stalin’s comments to the ambassadors on 15 August connected the southern battlefield with that diplomatic effort. He acknowledged severe strain in Ukraine and anticipated the loss of Nikolaev. His statements about the total number of enemy divisions and comparative aircraft and tank strength were contemporary claims, not verified statistical balances. More concretely, he requested armour plate and aluminium and argued that Arkhangelsk offered advantages over Vladivostok, citing the Japanese complication and the long Trans-Siberian railway journey. Even the form in which aid should be supplied depended on transportation: shipping material for Soviet manufacture might be more practical than moving complete heavy vehicles. [13] [14]

What widening meant on 12 August

By 12 August, the campaign demanded several kinds of operation at once. Army Group North sought to breach prepared positions while protecting communications against a counterstroke. In the south, German and Romanian forces pursued withdrawing armies and approached a coastal defence sustained through a different transport system. Soviet commanders attempted to recover initiative with damaged formations while releasing some positions and retaining others. The resulting competition for staff work, reserves and transport helps explain how a successful penetration could expand the victor’s commitments. The widening of the war lay in this multiplication of tasks as well as in the length of the front. Leningrad had not yet been cut off by the land blockade that began in September. Odessa had not fallen; its defence would continue into October. On 12 August, commanders and residents had to act without knowing how either struggle would end, or which routes would remain available to them. The immediate record shows uncertainty alongside deliberate action: daily objectives around Staraya Russa, orders to recover equipment during withdrawal, factories continuing essential work and diplomatic requests shaped by shipping routes. Germany and its allies retained the capacity to impose grave defeats, but their successes were producing obligations as well as opportunities. The next chapter turns to Gomel, where the contest over Army Group Centre’s southern flank would connect these dispersed pressures to the coming struggle for Ukraine. [4]

sourceMethod: Numbered citations lead to the sources below; each entry lists the passages cited and links back to its first use. Numbered references link to the bibliography and return to their first use. Specific document, paragraph and page locators accompany the references. Soviet military records were read in Russian transcription from the published General Staff collections; English descriptions are paraphrases by the atlas, and archival identifiers are those printed in the collections, not claims of direct archival inspection. Orders establish intentions; situation reports contain contemporary information, estimates and gaps. U.S. Army retrospective studies are read critically alongside Soviet records and other scholarship. Publisher excerpts are cited only for inspected passages. Testimony is distinguished from contemporary reporting. Dates in titles anchor the chronology; subsequent developments are dated explicitly. The atlas layers are qualified regional interpretations; their boundaries and arrows are not independent evidence of exact control or unit positions.
